title: The Captured Internet

sourceEvidence.locator: The Internet can function while its public world thins
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The book begins from a disturbing possibility: networks, search, messaging, video, and personal assistants may operate perfectly while the human world carried by them becomes harder to trust or challenge. More content is produced for ranking systems, more selection occurs through institutions answerable to someone other than the user, and generative abundance lowers the cost of assertion without similarly lowering the cost of verification. Technical success can therefore coexist with civic impoverishment.

sourceEvidence.locator: The Internet can function while its public world thins
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The familiar story of an innocent decentralized Internet captured by corporations is only partly correct. Early openness emerged from public funding, universities, contractors, standards bodies, infrastructure, skilled communities, and administrators. It worked under conditions of subsidy and selective participation. Open protocols solved interoperability and permissionless application development, but not identity, discovery, spam, moderation, financing, reputation, or collective decision-making. Capture grew through unresolved governance problems rather than through a single departure from an originally power-free network.

sourceEvidence.locator: Why platforms won—and became hidden constitutions
sourceEvidence.excerpt: Platforms integrated services people genuinely needed: hosting, persistent accounts, contact networks, mobile access, payments, search, recommendation, moderation, and security. Network effects made integrated systems increasingly difficult to leave. The social graph migrated from hyperlinks and address books into proprietary databases, while independent websites absorbed platform analytics, authentication, advertising, and distribution. Centralization was useful coordination before it became sovereignty.

sourceEvidence.locator: Why platforms won—and became hidden constitutions
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The constitutional problem appears when one provider owns identity, relationships, archives, ranking, revenue, evidence, rulemaking, enforcement, and appeal. Users create culture and data; moderators perform civic labor; creators attract audiences; yet the accumulated community becomes a corporate asset. Power is not confined to executives. Founders, investors, moderators, algorithms, advertisers, influential users, and infrastructure operators exercise different forms of control. Calling the result a service agreement obscures the fact that it governs membership, visibility, livelihood, and speech.

hook: The internet can work beautifully while the communities inside it lose the power to question its rules.
readerPromise: Understand platform power through the governance problems that made its useful concentration possible.
protectedRevelations: Detailed layered alternatives, governance designs and final prescriptions.
visualPlan: Show active human community and functioning connections together, avoiding a generic broken-internet image.
Keep useful integrated services beside the accumulating authority to set rules.
Focus one ranking decision on whose contribution becomes visible rather than animating a full recommendation engine.
